articles.title: Binary to Hex: The Group-of-Four Trick, With Examples
articles.excerpt: Converting binary to hexadecimal looks like math homework, but it is really just a lookup. Once you know one rule, you can do it in your head. A hex digit has 16 possible values, and four bits have ex…
articles.body: Converting binary to hexadecimal looks like math homework, but it is really just a lookup. Once you know one rule, you can do it in your head. The rule: group in fours, from the right A hex digit has 16 possible values, and four bits have exactly 16 patterns (2^4 = 16). So one hex digit stands for one group of four bits. Group the bits in fours, starting from the right . Pad the leftmost group with zeros if it has fewer than four bits. Replace each group with its hex digit (0-9, then A-F). Join the digits. Example 1: a byte 10110101 splits cleanly into 1011 0101 . 1011 is B (11 in decimal) and 0101 is 5. Answer: B5 . Example 2: when the length is not a multiple of four 100111100 has 9 bits. Group from the right: 1 0011 1100 . Pad the lonely 1 to 0001 , then look each group up: 1, 3, C.

articles.body: EasyRSA needs a certificate-state inventory beyond the CA directory EasyRSA is a command-line PKI utility for creating a certificate authority, signing certificate requests, renewing certificates, revoking them, and generating certificate revocation lists. Its files are familiar to administrators, but the meaning of a certificate is spread across the request, serial number, issued files, renewal history, revocation database, and published CRL. A count-only ZoomEye query on 2026-11-25 at 03:47 UTC used sub_type=all , page 1, and page size 1. http.body="EasyRSA" returned 626 matches. The query is available in ZoomEye . A body match can be documentation, a tutorial, a paste, or a page about a deployment. It is not a count of exposed EasyRSA PKI directories.

articles.title: 3,954 of 4,000 replies right, 4,000 of 4,000 states exact: a host-side layer on Gemini 3.8 Flash, checkable in seconds
articles.excerpt: On one job of 4,000 requests, Gemini 3.8 Flash's own replies were exactly right 3,954 times (98.85 percent). The state the host held was exactly right on all 4,000 steps. The model was not changed. Th…
articles.body: On one job of 4,000 requests, Gemini 3.8 Flash's own replies were exactly right 3,954 times (98.85 percent). The state the host held was exactly right on all 4,000 steps. The model was not changed. The 46 replies that were not exactly right all left out the same thing, and a fixed rule on the host completed them. The 4,000-step figures can be recomputed from the saved replies in a few seconds, with no key; every other figure points to the page and run file that holds it. AXI is a layer on the host side, between a model and the state it edits. The architecture is by Rajnish Choubey ; the tests were built and run by Shalendra Gaur , working with an AI coding assistant that is a tool, not an author.

articles.body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science Amateur Astronomer? Be a… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova . These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project! Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.

articles.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
articles.excerpt: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission wi…
articles.body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

articles.title: 1st-ever detection of a dying star's 'final nuclear heartbeat' challenges what we know about our sun's eventual death
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have caught a rare transitional phase at the end of a star's life, a fossilized remnant of stellar death throes, that could change our picture of the sun's final days.
articles.body: As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper. New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

articles.body: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star. NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A (Cas A) in this high-resolution, mid-infrared image released on Nov. 23, 2026. Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets.

articles.body: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. From left, technicians Chad Cook and Seth Harvey install the high-resolution microscopic imager – part of the seven-camera DragonCam science imaging suite – onto NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, on Nov. 6, 2026. NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Ed Whitman First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan ’s surface at multiple scales during flight and while on the ground.

articles.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
articles.excerpt: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is add…
articles.body: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers. As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening.
